definition.text: Workspace (card 3.4, area Core Agent) is this repo's own reference-model bucket for three things a unit of agent work reads and writes while it runs -- files, memory, and shared state -- sitting between the isolation boundary that contains a run (3.3 Runtime/Sandbox) and the tools a run can call (3.5 Tool Interface). This is a proposed definition, not a sourced one: unlike 3.3 Runtime/Sandbox, whose 'a unit of work runs isolated' requirement is stated directly in this repo's own PASS.md (F-b3-18), PASS.md contains zero occurrences of the word 'memory' anywhere and has no dedicated workspace section (checked directly against the file), so nothing in this repo's own current-state baseline defines 'Workspace' as one thing the way it defines Runtime/Sandbox. The three parts this card bundles are each independently named in the sources found below (a static, human-authored context file; a runtime-written memory record; a durable per-run state snapshot), but no source treats the three as a single governed element the way this card's name implies.

standards.role: Names the static, human-authored half of Workspace: a single Markdown file (or one nested per subproject, closest wins) placed at the project root that a coding agent reads at the start of a session for build/test/style/context instructions it would otherwise have to re-derive or be told over chat.
standards.covers: Never uses the words 'memory' or 'state' anywhere across the full page text of its own specification site (checked directly by fetching https://agents.md/ in full on 2026-09-10: zero occurrences of either word). Its own FAQ treats the file as documentation a person edits between sessions ('Treat AGENTS.md as living documentation'), not as a store an agent writes to at runtime or a place multiple agents share live state through. So this badge reaches roughly one of the card's three named parts (files) and not the other two (memory, shared state).

evidence.text: AGENTS.md's own site frames the file as extra, human-supplied context for build/test/conventions that an agent reads -- the same framing an earlier research pass for a different card (3.3 Runtime/Sandbox) reached independently when ruling AGENTS.md out as an environment-declaration standard: it 'provides a dedicated, predictable location for the minimal, human-authored context that LLM coding assistants' need.

evidence.quote: AGENTS.md complements this by containing the extra, sometimes detailed context coding agents need: build steps, tests, and conventions
provides a dedicated, predictable location for the minimal, human-authored context that LLM coding assistants

tools.name: AGENTS.md
tools.note: The spec's own reference convention: one Markdown file at repo root (or nested per subproject, closest wins) that a person edits and an agent reads at session start. This repo has no file named AGENTS.md anywhere in its tree (checked directly on 2026-09-10, whole-repo search) despite this card naming it as the standard badge.

evidence.text: AGENTS.md's own onboarding step is exactly this: create the file at the repo root, and agents pick up nested copies automatically as they walk the directory tree.

evidence.quote: Create an AGENTS.md file at the root of the repository.

tools.name: CLAUDE.md files (Claude Code)
tools.note: This repo's actual root-level persistent-instructions file (checked directly: CLAUDE.md at the repo root, and a second copy under ref_arch/) -- the same genre of file AGENTS.md standardizes, but under Anthropic's own vendor-specific filename rather than the cross-vendor name this card's standard badge names.

evidence.text: Claude Code's own docs describe CLAUDE.md files as the human-written half of its two-part memory system.

evidence.quote: CLAUDE.md files are markdown files that give Claude persistent instructions for a project, your personal workflow, or your entire organization.

tools.name: Claude Code auto memory
tools.note: The agent-written half of the same system: notes Claude saves itself between sessions, stored outside this git repository in the operator's own Claude Code config directory -- not something this repo's own build checks in or claims as part of its target architecture.

evidence.text: Claude Code's docs describe auto memory as knowledge the agent accumulates for itself, without the user writing anything.

evidence.quote: Auto memory lets Claude accumulate knowledge across sessions without you writing anything.

tools.name: LangGraph checkpointer
tools.note: Snapshots full run state to a pluggable store keyed by a thread id so a run can pause, resume, rewind or branch -- a durable-execution/state-recovery mechanism (this repo's own 4.3 State & Recovery / cap-state-persistence territory) rather than a workspace-context mechanism, even though it is the closest real, named tool found to this card's 'shared state' wording. Not used here.

evidence.text: LangGraph's checkpointer is named prior art for durable, resumable run state, snapshotted after every step and keyed by thread.

evidence.quote: LangGraph checkpoints turn a graph into a durable program: after every super-step the full state is snapshotted to a Checkpointer (in-memory, SQLite, or Postgres), keyed by thread_id

tools.name: Portable Agent Memory (protocol proposal)
tools.note: An academic proposal (arXiv) for provenance-verified memory transfer across agents built by different vendors -- the nearest thing found to a standard for this card's 'shared state' component, and explicitly not a ratified one. Not used here.

evidence.text: The paper itself frames the gap it is trying to fill: tool access and task delegation both have ratified cross-vendor standards; memory portability does not.

evidence.quote: Portable Agent Memory addresses a critical gap in the emerging agent interoperability stack: while MCP standardizes tool access and A2A standardizes task delegation, no prior protocol provides verified memory portability.

landscape.text: Tooling splits along the card's own three-part name rather than converging on one thing. For files/context, the pattern that has actually converged across vendors is a single, human-edited Markdown file loaded automatically at session start: AGENTS.md's site walks through exactly that step, 'Create an AGENTS.md file at the root of the repository,' and Claude Code implements the same idea under its own vendor-specific name (CLAUDE.md). For memory, the industry treats it as a separate, runtime-written layer built on embedding retrieval rather than a static file: 'Agent memory systems typically embed queries and stored memories, rank candidate memories by cosine similarity, and place the top-ranked memories into the model context.' Distinct again from either file is the more basic question of what sits inside a running context window at all -- Anthropic's own engineering guidance names this its own technique, compaction, defined as 'taking a conversation nearing the context window limit, summarizing its contents, and reinitiating a new context window with the summary.' For shared state specifically, the closest real, named tooling found says plainly that it does not do that across machines: Claude Code's own memory docs state 'Auto memory is machine-local. All worktrees and subdirectories within the same git repository share one auto memory directory. Files are not shared across machines or cloud environments,' and the closest durable-state mechanism found, LangGraph's checkpointer, snapshots full run state to a store rather than exposing a live workspace multiple agents write into concurrently: 'LangGraph checkpoints turn a graph into a durable program: after every super-step the full state is snapshotted to a Checkpointer (in-memory, SQLite, or Postgres), keyed by thread_id.' And no ratified standard governs sharing memory across agents from different vendors at all: 'Portable Agent Memory addresses a critical gap in the emerging agent interoperability stack: while MCP standardizes tool access and A2A standardizes task delegation, no prior protocol provides verified memory portability.'

evidence.quote: Create an AGENTS.md file at the root of the repository.
Agent memory systems typically embed queries and stored memories, rank candidate memories by cosine similarity, and place the top-ranked memories into the model context.
Compaction is the practice of taking a conversation nearing the context window limit, summarizing its contents, and reinitiating a new context window with the summary.
Auto memory is machine-local. All worktrees and subdirectories within the same git repository share one auto memory directory. Files are not shared across machines or cloud environments.
LangGraph checkpoints turn a graph into a durable program: after every super-step the full state is snapshotted to a Checkpointer (in-memory, SQLite, or Postgres), keyed by thread_id

Portable Agent Memory addresses a critical gap in the emerging agent interoperability stack: while MCP standardizes tool access and A2A standardizes task delegation, no prior protocol provides verified memory portability.

usage.text: No source found describes a caller invoking Workspace through an explicit API call the way this repo's other capabilities are called; the two real, named implementations closest to it both load automatically rather than being called. AGENTS.md is picked up walking the directory tree: 'Agents automatically read the nearest file in the directory tree, so the closest one takes precedence.' Claude Code's two mechanisms load the same way, without a caller choosing to invoke either one per turn: 'Claude Code has two complementary memory systems. Both are loaded at the start of every conversation.'

evidence.quote: Agents automatically read the nearest file in the directory tree, so the closest one takes precedence
Claude Code has two complementary memory systems. Both are loaded at the start of every conversation.

gaps.what: This card's standard badge names AGENTS.md, but this repo has no file named AGENTS.md anywhere in its tree (checked directly across the whole repository on 2026-09-10: zero matches). It has two files named CLAUDE.md instead (the repo root and ref_arch/), a different, vendor-specific convention for the same genre of static, human-authored context.
gaps.why_it_matters: A 'built' status next to a standard badge this repo's own files don't actually carry overstates how governed this element is -- and even where the badge does apply, per this card's own standards.covers, it reaches only one of the three parts ('files') the card's own name promises ('files, memory, shared state').
gaps.research_query: does this repo intend to add or symlink an AGENTS.md file, and should the standard badge on 3.4 change if it does not

gaps.what: This repo's own card/example gap analysis (docs/reference/card-example-gaps.md) states directly that no example area exercises a mutable shared workspace, and that mounts in this repo are read-only with sealed, write-once output. The same document separately notes that 8 of this repo's 40 reference-model cards have no proof in any of the seven example areas, and that Workspace is one of only 3 of those 8 marked 'built' rather than 'planned' -- so, unlike most of the unproven cards, its silence in the examples is not explained by build status.
gaps.why_it_matters: 'Built' should mean the element is demonstrated somewhere in this repo, not only named in the reference model; by this repo's own analysis, Workspace currently has neither a working mutable-shared-state mechanism nor an example that reaches it.
gaps.research_query: does any harness or example in this repo implement a writable, multi-run-shared filesystem, memory area, or workspace

gaps.what: Memory, one third of this card's own definition, is absent from PASS.md (this repo's current-state document contains zero occurrences of the word 'memory') and exists in this repo only as a proposed target contract: cap-state-persistence's cap-memory sub-skill states its own purpose exists 'because TARGET requires the gaps in that baseline to be made up,' and this repo's own TARGET.md states plainly that PASS.md's list is a limited baseline whose gaps still need to be made up and solved (T-t4-03).
gaps.why_it_matters: Marking 3.4 'built' implies its memory component works today; this repo's own documents instead describe memory as an acknowledged target-state gap with a proposed schema, not a measured capability.
gaps.research_query: has cap-state-persistence's memory-item contract (remember/recall/expire) been implemented and exercised by any harness, or does it remain schema-only

gaps.what: The 'files' part of this card's own definition (a read-only context mount) is the same seam 3.3 Runtime/Sandbox already owns -- external prior art found treats mounting a skill/context directory read-only as a sandbox/isolation concern enforced by the kernel, not a separate workspace mechanism. And the closest real, named tool found to this card's 'shared state' wording, LangGraph's checkpointer, snapshots full run state keyed by a thread id -- a durable-execution/state-recovery mechanism, which is 4.3 State & Recovery's and cap-state-persistence's territory, not a live mutable workspace multiple agents write into.
gaps.why_it_matters: If Workspace bundles two other cards' actual seams rather than naming a distinct capability, treating it as a fourth thing risks double-counting effort, or leaving a real component with no clear owner.
gaps.research_query: does cap-isolation (3.3) or cap-state-persistence (4.3 / base.4) already claim ownership of the context-mount and memory-item pieces this card also names

gaps.what: No source found names a ratified, cross-vendor standard for sharing or moving agent memory or workspace state across agents built by different vendors, unlike this repo's other Core Agent cards, which each name one (AGENTS.md here; MCP for 3.5 Tool Interface). The closest found is an unratified academic protocol proposal, Portable Agent Memory.
gaps.why_it_matters: Even a correctly-scoped Workspace standard badge would only ever cover the files third of the definition until (if ever) a memory/shared-state standard emerges industry-wide; the remaining gap is not just this repo's citation work.
gaps.research_query: has Portable Agent Memory or a similar proposal been adopted by any production agent framework since 2026-09
